modules.title: The Benefit & Your Role
modules.summary: What the Medicaid meal benefit is, what you may say about it, and the four things every call has to establish.

blocks.html:
This is a meal delivery benefit that is already included in the consumer's Medicaid. Up to 3 meals a day, at no cost to them, delivered to their door, with no change to their coverage.

You are not selling it. You are not signing anyone up. You confirm four things and hand the consumer to a screener.

The four things:

  1. They still receive Medicaid
  2. Their borough
  3. Their ZIP code
  4. All of it again, as a double confirm

Then you get their okay and bring the screener on.

blocks.title: What you may say
blocks.html: Up to 3 meals a day · at no cost · included in your Medicaid · delivered to your doorstep · no change to your coverage · you're already approved. All of that is approved wording.

blocks.title: What you may never say
blocks.html: That it costs anything. That their coverage changes. A delivery date. A dollar amount. A specific menu. The screener handles all of that — and two of those are simply untrue.

blocks.question: What is this benefit?
choices: A new insurance plan you're enrolling them in
A meal delivery benefit already included in their Medicaid
blocks.explanation: Already included in their Medicaid. Nothing is being sold or changed.

lessons.title: The call is short — much shorter than you think

blocks.html: Across 3,263 real calls, a typical one runs about a minute and a half. When a consumer brushes you off and the agent doesn't come straight back, the median call is 27 seconds.
That is the whole reason the script says GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE after every rebuttal. It isn't a style note. You have seconds.

blocks.title: Consumers answer in two or three words
blocks.html: “Yes.” “No.” “What?” “Who's this?” That is normal on this campaign. Don't mistake a short answer for rudeness, and don't fill the silence with a speech.

blocks.question: A consumer says “not interested” four seconds into the call. What does the data say happens next?
choices: Most agents rebut and recover the call
Most of these calls end within seconds
The consumer usually asks a question
It makes no difference to the outcome
blocks.explanation: 97.5% of calls where “not interested” comes up never reach a transfer. The window is tiny.

blocks.html: New York City Medicaid recipients across the five boroughs. Many are older. Many are hard of hearing. Many speak English as a second language. A lot of them have had several calls like this already.
Expect to repeat yourself, and expect suspicion — the most common single reaction on these calls is some version of “What?”

blocks.title: Slow down rather than speed up
blocks.html: If someone can't hear you, talking faster loses the call. The verifications are short; say them clearly and wait.

blocks.question: A consumer asks you to repeat yourself twice in the first fifteen seconds. What's the right move?
choices: Transfer them to the screener early
blocks.explanation: Hard of hearing is normal here, not a brush-off.

lessons.title: What the screener does, and what you don't

blocks.html: The screener sets up the service. They cover delivery, menus, timing and anything specific. Your job ends when they're talking to the consumer.

So when a consumer asks “when do the meals come?” or “can I pick what I get?”, the honest and compliant answer is the same: the screener will go over that — and then straight back to your verification.

blocks.title: Guessing is how agents get in trouble
blocks.html: Promising a delivery date or a specific menu is a compliance failure even when you're trying to be helpful. You genuinely don't know, and the consumer remembers what you told them.

blocks.question: “When will my first delivery come?”
choices: “The screener will go over all of that with you — I just need to confirm…”
blocks.explanation: You don't know, and the script sends it to the screener.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hey, good morning, am I speaking with Maria?

lines.speaker: consumer
lines.text: Yes, who's this?

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hey Maria, this is Nate, I'm with America's Health on a recorded line. We were just giving you a quick call today about the Medicaid meal service for you and your family. I just need to confirm you ARE still receiving Medicaid, correct?

lines.speaker: consumer
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Okay perfect, and you're still in the Bronx, with the zip code 10457, correct?

lines.speaker: consumer
lines.text: That's right.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Okay LAST question here, JUST to double confirm, you ARE receiving Medicaid and you ARE still in the Bronx, correct?

lines.speaker: consumer
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Perfect, that's everything I need. The screener is coming on the line now to help you set that up, once that's finished they'll have you on your way, okay?

lines.speaker: consumer
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: (warm handoff naming the consumer, borough and ZIP)

blocks.html: Four verifications, a permission, a handoff. Under ninety seconds. That's the job.

blocks.question: How many separate times is Medicaid confirmed on a correct call?
choices: Twice — the first ask and the double confirm
blocks.explanation: The first ask, then again in the double confirm before the transfer.

questions.question: What is the meal benefit?
choices: A new plan you enrol them in
A benefit already included in their Medicaid

questions.question: How many meals a day may you mention?
questions.explanation: Up to 3 meals a day is approved wording.

questions.question: Which of these may you NOT say?
choices: There's no change to your coverage
questions.explanation: Delivery dates belong to the screener and you don't know them.

questions.question: A typical call on this campaign runs about…
questions.explanation: Around a minute and a half. Brush-off calls that aren't rebutted die at 27 seconds.

questions.question: What are the four things you confirm?
choices: Medicaid, borough, ZIP, then all of it again
Borough, ZIP, meals wanted, delivery day

questions.question: Who handles delivery and menu questions?
questions.explanation: The screener. Redirect and go back to verifying.

questions.question: A consumer answers “yes” in one word. That is…
choices: A reason to slow the pitch
questions.explanation: Two or three word answers are the norm here.

questions.question: Why does the script say “don't stop or pause”?
choices: Because brush-off calls end in seconds if you hesitate
questions.explanation: 27 seconds is the median when a brush-off goes unrebutted.

modules.title: The Medicaid Question
modules.summary: The one question the whole campaign rests on, its three-way branch, the ten qualifying plans, and the boroughs.

blocks.html:
Everything on this campaign rests on one question:

“I just need to confirm you ARE still receiving Medicaid, correct?”

blocks.title: Skipping it is not a missed step — it's treated as fraud
blocks.html: Management's position is unambiguous. Transferring someone without ever asking whether they have Medicaid is the most serious failure on this campaign, and the simulator fails the call outright no matter how good the rest was.
It is also not hypothetical. On an offshore floor that was shut down over it, 88% of transfers never asked the question. On the named floor it still happens on about 1 in 16 transfers.
Ask it. Wait for the answer. The whole thing takes four seconds.

blocks.question: You've confirmed the borough and ZIP, the consumer is friendly, and you never got around to the Medicaid question. What now?
choices: Ask it before you do anything else
blocks.explanation: No Medicaid question, no transfer. Ever.

blocks.html: Three answers, three paths.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: I just need to confirm you ARE still receiving Medicaid, correct?

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: YES → continue to the borough

lines.speaker: consumer
lines.text: No, I don't have that.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Oh there must have been a mistake, thank you for your time, have a great day. (END AND CODE AS DQ)

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: I DON'T KNOW → use the fallback question

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Okay, well let me ask you this, when you go to the doctor, do you have to pay anything, or is it usually free?

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: Free / from the state → continue. Copays → DQ line.

blocks.title: “I don't know” is not a dead end
blocks.html:
It's the most misplayed answer on the campaign. People genuinely don't know what their coverage is called — but they know whether they pay at the doctor. That's what the fallback question is for.

Roughly one consumer in five doesn't know. Learn this branch cold.

blocks.question: “I'm not sure what I have.” What's your next sentence?
choices: “No problem, let me get you to the screener.”
“Okay, well let me ask you this — when you go to the doctor, do you have to pay anything, or is it usually free?”
blocks.explanation: The copay fallback. Free or from the state qualifies; copays is a DQ.

lessons.title: When they name a plan instead

blocks.html: Plenty of consumers don't say “Medicaid” — they say the name of their plan. These ten count as Medicaid:
Healthfirst · Fidelis · MetroPlus · Emblem · VNS · Molina · UHC Community · Anthem HealthPlus · Aetna Better Health · Amida Care

blocks.title: A bare brand name is not enough
blocks.html: “United”, “Aetna” or “Anthem” on their own do not qualify. Those companies sell Medicaid plans and ordinary plans. You need the Medicaid version — “UHC Community”, “Aetna Better Health”, “Anthem HealthPlus” — or a plain yes to the Medicaid question.
And Medicare is not Medicaid. They sound alike and plenty of consumers mix them up. Medicare on its own does not qualify for this benefit.

blocks.question: “I've got Aetna.” What do you do?
choices: Continue — Aetna is on the list
Establish whether it's Aetna Better Health or an ordinary Aetna plan
blocks.explanation: Aetna Better Health qualifies; a plain Aetna plan doesn't. Establish which.

blocks.html: The service covers Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and Staten Island. Nothing else.

They sayOutcome
Bronx / Brooklyn / Manhattan / Queens / Staten IslandContinue
Long IslandOutside the area — DQ
Long Island CityThat's Queens — continue
Yonkers, New Jersey, upstateOutside the area — DQ
“New York” / “NYC”Too vague — ask which borough

blocks.title: Long Island and Long Island City are different places
blocks.html: One is outside the service area and one is in Queens. Hear the difference before you DQ someone who qualifies, or transfer someone who doesn't.
The ZIP code comes with the borough in the same breath, and it's skipped on a quarter of real calls. It's one short question — ask it.

blocks.question: “I'm in Long Island City.”
choices: Ask them to be more specific
blocks.explanation: Long Island City is in Queens and qualifies.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Okay LAST question here, JUST to double confirm, you ARE receiving Medicaid and you ARE still in (their borough), correct?

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: (wait for the answer — then the transfer ask)

blocks.html: Medicaid and borough, together, as the final question before the transfer. It's skipped or rushed on 38% of real calls.

blocks.title: Why it exists
blocks.html: The first time you ask, people answer on autopilot while they work out who you are. The second time, they're listening. A meaningful number correct themselves — and that correction is the difference between a clean transfer and one that gets docked.

blocks.question: Is the double confirm the same question as the first Medicaid ask?
choices: No — it's a separate, deliberate last check of both facts
blocks.explanation: A separate ask covering Medicaid AND borough, every call.

questions.question: What happens if you transfer without ever asking about Medicaid?
choices: Automatic fail — it's treated as fraud
questions.explanation: The most serious failure on the campaign.

questions.question: “I don't know” — what's the fallback question?
choices: Ask whether they pay anything at the doctor
questions.explanation: Free or from the state qualifies; copays is a DQ.

questions.question: A consumer pays copays at the doctor. Outcome?
choices: Transfer and let the screener check

questions.question: Which qualifies as Medicaid?
questions.explanation: Amida Care is on the list. Bare parent brands are not.

questions.question: Medicare with no Medicaid?
Long Island?
Long Island City?
A consumer says just “New York”. What do you do?
questions.explanation: Not specific enough — pin down the borough.

questions.question: How many plans are on the qualifying list?
The double confirm covers…
questions.explanation: Both, as a separate last question.

questions.question: Roughly how often does a consumer not know whether they're on Medicaid?
questions.explanation: Which is why the fallback question matters.

questions.question: How often is the ZIP skipped on real calls?

modules.title: The Script, Line by Line
modules.summary: Every line in order, and the step that breaks on a third of real calls.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hey, good morning (Customer's Name)?

lines.speaker: consumer
lines.text: Yeah?

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hey, good morning (Customer's Name), this is _______, I'm with America's Health on a recorded line. We were just giving you a quick call today about the Medicaid meal service for you and your family. I just need to confirm you ARE still receiving Medicaid, correct?

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: (WAIT for the answer)

blocks.html: Four things in one breath: who you're speaking to, your company, the recorded line, and what the call is about — then straight into the Medicaid question.

blocks.title: Don't lose the recorded line
blocks.html: It's missing from the opening on about 1 in 20 real calls, and skipped or rushed on far more. It costs you two seconds.

blocks.question: Which belongs in the opening?
choices: That the call is on a recorded line
blocks.explanation: Name, company, recorded line, what the call is about.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Okay perfect, and you're still in (Customer's Borough), with the zip code (Customer's Zip Code), correct?

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: (WAIT)

blocks.html: One sentence, two facts. The borough decides whether they're in the service area; the ZIP goes to the screener.

blocks.title: The ZIP is the most skipped verification
blocks.html: Missing on 24.7% of real calls, and rushed on another 18.7%. It's in the same sentence as the borough — there's no reason for it to go missing except speed.

blocks.question: The consumer gives the borough but not the ZIP. What do you do?
choices: Move on — borough is the important one
Ask for the ZIP before continuing
Read them the ZIP from the screen and move on
blocks.explanation: Both, every call.

lessons.title: Permission to transfer — the broken step

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Perfect, that's everything I need. The screener is coming on the line now to help you set that up, once that's finished, they'll have you on your way, okay?

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: AFFIRM — MUST GET PERMISSION TO TRANSFER

blocks.title: A third of real calls skip this entirely
blocks.html: Permission was never obtained on 32.3% of calls, and rushed on another 19.9%. It is the single biggest procedural gap on this campaign — 446 calls in the sample were transferred with no okay from the consumer.
The word “okay?” is in the script for a reason. Say it, then stop talking until you hear an answer. Silence is not permission, and neither is the consumer still being on the line.

blocks.question: You say “…they'll have you on your way, okay?” and hear nothing. What now?
choices: Ask again and wait for an answer
blocks.explanation: No answer is not permission.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hey agent, I have (Customer's Name) in (Customer's Borough), the zip code for them is (Customer's Zip). Can you take the call from here? Okay, I'll drop the line and let you two finish up, you both have a great day!

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: (wait until they're talking, then drop)

blocks.html: Three facts in the handoff: who, which borough, which ZIP. This is the step agents are best at — 83% do it properly — so it's mostly a matter of not letting it slip.

blocks.question: What goes in the handoff?
blocks.explanation: All three, then wait for them to engage before dropping.

blocks.html: When someone doesn't qualify, there is one approved line:

blocks.objection: No Medicaid / copays / outside the boroughs
blocks.response: Oh there must have been a mistake, thank you for your time, have a great day.
blocks.coach_note: Warm, short, and then end the call. No arguing, no trying to find a way around it, no transferring to see what the screener says.

blocks.title: A DQ is a correct outcome, not a loss
blocks.html: 169 consumers in the sample should have been DQ'd. 99 were caught. 38 were transferred anyway — mostly people who said plainly they don't have Medicaid. Catching a DQ is a good call; transferring one is the failure.

blocks.question: “No, I don't have Medicaid.” What do you do?
choices: Ask if they have Medicare instead
Read the DQ line and end the call
Transfer and let the screener decide
blocks.explanation: Read the line, code it DQ, move on.

questions.question: What must be in your opening?
Which step is skipped most often?
questions.explanation: 32.3% — the biggest gap on the campaign.

questions.question: Silence after the transfer ask means…
The ZIP is skipped on roughly…
What three facts go in the handoff?
A consumer doesn't qualify. You should…
choices: Read the DQ line and end
questions.explanation: The approved DQ line, then end.

questions.question: How many consumers in the sample were transferred despite not qualifying?
questions.explanation: 38 of the 169 who should have been DQ'd.

questions.question: When can you drop the line on the handoff?
choices: As soon as the screener answers
Once the screener and consumer are talking

modules.title: Rebuttals — Where the Money Is
modules.summary: The eight approved rebuttals, which objections actually lose calls, and why speed matters more here than anywhere else.

blocks.html: This is measured from 3,263 real calls — 1,196 that transferred and 2,067 that didn't. For the first time we can say not just how often an objection comes up, but what it costs.

ObjectionComes up onCalls lost
Not interested14.9%97.5%
I don't need it8.5%89.6%
I'm busy / call me back10.6%82.6%
Who are you with?13.5%68.9%
I already have it4.0%63.1%
What is this?19.8%51.9%

blocks.title: The most common objection is the safest
blocks.html: “What is this?” comes up on one call in five and agents handle it well. The dangerous ones are the brush-offs — less frequent, far more expensive.
And on more than half the “not interested” calls, no rebuttal was attempted at all. That's not a skill gap. That's agents letting the call go.

blocks.question: Which objection loses the highest share of the calls it appears on?
blocks.explanation: 97.5%. And over half the time nobody even tries a rebuttal.

blocks.html: Real consumers say it like this: “No, thank you.”, “I'm not interested.”

blocks.response: I understand, but groceries are NOT getting any cheaper. You are ALREADY approved for up to three meals at NO cost and this is INCLUDED in your Medicaid. I just need to confirm... (GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE)
blocks.coach_note: Don't acknowledge the no and pause — that's the pause the call dies in. Lead with groceries not getting cheaper, land “already approved” and “no cost”, and go straight back to the verification.

blocks.response: Oh let me assure you this will be SUPER brief, I just have 3 SUPER quick questions and I'll bring the screener on. I just need to confirm... (GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE)
blocks.coach_note: Promise brevity and prove it. Three quick questions, then the screener. Agents who stop to arrange a callback lose 82.6% of these.

blocks.response: I understand, but with groceries and the cost of living going up, having three meals delivered at NO cost can take a little pressure off your grocery budget. And if you don't personally need them, you could ALWAYS give them to someone in your family or someone who could use the help. You're already approved for it, so there's nothing extra you're paying for. I just need to confirm... (GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE)
blocks.coach_note: The give-it-to-someone-else angle is the one that works — it removes the need to admit they need help. 89.6% of these calls are lost, so this rebuttal is worth knowing word for word.

blocks.title: 27 seconds
blocks.html: When no rebuttal comes, the median brush-off call lasts 27 seconds. When one does, 43. You are not having a conversation — you are getting one sentence in before the line goes dead.

blocks.question: A consumer says “I don't need it, give it to someone who needs it more.” What does the approved rebuttal do?
choices: Agrees and ends the call politely
Points out they could pass the meals to family, and that they're already approved
Asks why they don't need it
blocks.explanation: It removes the need to admit they need help, which is what the objection is really about.

blocks.html: The most common objection on the campaign, on 19.8% of calls: “What?”, “What is this about?”

blocks.objection: What is this / Why are you calling me?
blocks.response: This is a meal delivery benefit included in your Medicaid. It provides up to 3 meals daily at no cost, and no change to coverage. I just need to confirm... (GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE)
blocks.coach_note: Short and concrete. Meal delivery, included in their Medicaid, no cost, no change to coverage — then straight back to verifying.

blocks.response: Oh I'm with America's Health. We work with over 25 different health insurance providers. We're just here to facilitate your free review. I just need to confirm... (GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE)
blocks.coach_note: Name the company and move. This one is handled well on real calls and rarely needs more than a sentence.

blocks.objection: How much is this going to cost me?
blocks.response: Oh this is ALREADY included in your Medicaid. There is NO cost to you and there is NO change to your coverage. You're ALREADY preapproved for up to 3 meals a day, delivered to your doorstep, I just need to activate it. I just need to confirm... (GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE)
blocks.coach_note: The honest answer is the strong one: nothing. It's already included. Note this objection barely loses any calls — people ask it to check for a catch, and the plain answer satisfies them.

blocks.title: Why these are safe
blocks.html: These three are questions, not refusals. The consumer is engaging. Answer briefly and keep going — the mistake here is over-explaining, not under-explaining.

blocks.question: “How much is this going to cost me?”
choices: “Nothing — it's already included in your Medicaid, no cost and no change to your coverage.”
blocks.explanation: True, and it's approved wording.

blocks.html: On 4.0% of calls, and 63.1% of those are lost: “This is in reference to Medicaid meals. I already get.”

blocks.response: Yes of course, we were just calling about the EXTRA support, this isn't a replacement. There's actually been some NEW varieties that JUST released so MORE food coming in, we just need to activate it. I just need to confirm... (GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE)
blocks.coach_note: The key word is EXTRA. This isn't a replacement for what they have, and new varieties have just been released. Then back to the verification.

blocks.response: I understand, but there's actually some new varieties that JUST became available. From healthier options to hot, cold and frozen. Just let the screener know when we get there. I just need to confirm... (GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE)
blocks.coach_note: Don't argue about the food. New varieties, let the screener know what they prefer, keep moving.

blocks.objection: I already signed up with someone
blocks.response: Yes of course, we were just calling about the EXTRA support, this isn't a replacement. There's actually been some NEW varieties that JUST released so MORE food coming in, we just need to activate it. I just need to confirm... (GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE)
blocks.coach_note: Same shape as “I already have it” — this is extra support, and the screener sorts out the detail.

blocks.question: “I already get meals delivered.” What's the angle?
choices: This is EXTRA support, not a replacement, and new varieties just released
blocks.explanation: Extra, not instead of. Then straight back to the verification.

lessons.title: Suspicion, and where the script runs out

blocks.html: “I just don't understand why it's in my name. Is this a scam?” — suspicion is constant on these calls, and the strongest answer is simply naming who you are and what you need.

blocks.objection: Who are you with? (used for scam and personal-info pushback)
blocks.response: Oh I'm with America's Health. We work with over 25 different health insurance providers. We're just here to facilitate your free review. I just need to confirm... (GO RIGHT BACK WHERE YOU WERE, DON'T STOP OR PAUSE)
blocks.coach_note: You're not asking for a social security number, a bank account or a card. Say so — it's true and it's the fastest way to defuse this.

blocks.title: Two gaps in the script worth knowing
blocks.html:
“I was told I don't qualify” comes up on 1.7% of calls and loses 66% of them — and there is no approved rebuttal for it. Until there is, the closest approved line is the “what is this” explanation.

And there is no written do-not-call line on this script, unlike Medicare and ACA. Use a plain removal statement and end the call.
Both have been flagged to management. If an approved line lands for either, it goes into the script file and flows through automatically.

blocks.question: A consumer says to stop calling them. What do you do?
choices: Tell them they'll be removed, end the call, code DNC
blocks.explanation: Never rebuttal a do-not-call request.

questions.question: Which objection loses the most calls?
How often is no rebuttal even attempted on “not interested”?
choices: About a quarter of the time
questions.explanation: 286 of 541 occurrences got no response at all.

questions.question: Median length of a brush-off call with no rebuttal?
questions.explanation: 43 seconds when the agent does rebut.

questions.question: The “I don't need it” rebuttal works by…
choices: Suggesting they pass the meals to family and reminding them it's already approved
questions.explanation: It removes the need to admit they need help.

questions.question: “I already have it” — what's the key word?
What ends every rebuttal?
choices: Going right back to the verification without pausing

questions.question: “How much will this cost me?” is…
choices: One of the most dangerous objections
One of the least dangerous — the plain answer satisfies people
questions.explanation: It loses few calls. People are checking for a catch.

questions.question: Which objection currently has no approved rebuttal?
choices: I was told I don't qualify
questions.explanation: Flagged to management; use the “what is this” explanation meanwhile.

questions.question: A consumer swears at you but doesn't ask you to stop calling.
questions.explanation: Swearing is an objection, not a do-not-call request.

questions.question: “I'm busy, call me back” — best response?
choices: Promise brevity, three quick questions, keep going
questions.explanation: 82.6% of these are lost when the agent stops to arrange a callback.

modules.title: Compliance
modules.summary: What you may and may not say about a benefit the consumer already has, and the one failure treated as fraud.

blocks.html: Compliance applies to outbound, inbound, callbacks and immediate re-dials alike. The call where you already spoke to someone ten minutes ago is the one agents skip — do it anyway.

The nine required steps:

  1. Correct person
  2. America's Health
  3. On a recorded line
  4. The Medicaid meal service
  5. Ask about Medicaid
  6. Borough
  7. ZIP
  8. Double confirm
  9. Permission, then warm handoff

blocks.title: Two of these are failing badly on real calls
blocks.html: Permission to transfer is missing on 32.3% of calls. The recorded line is missing on 4.4%. Neither takes more than a few seconds.

blocks.question: A consumer rings back twenty minutes after you spoke. Which steps apply?
blocks.explanation: Every call means every call.

blocks.title: Never asking about Medicaid is treated as fraud
blocks.html: Not a missed step. Not points off. Management's position is that transferring someone without ever asking whether they have Medicaid is fraud, because it bills a transfer for a consumer nobody established as eligible.
An offshore floor was shut down over exactly this — 88% of their transfers never asked. On the named floor it still shows up on about 6% of transfers.
In the simulator, a transfer with no Medicaid question fails outright, whatever else you did well.

blocks.question: You had a great call, perfect rapport, consumer agreed to everything — but you never asked about Medicaid and transferred. Result?
choices: Points off for one missed step
blocks.explanation: Automatic fail. It's the one rule with no exceptions.

blocks.html:
All of this is approved, straight from the script:

  • Up to 3 meals a day
  • At no cost
  • Included in your Medicaid
  • Delivered to your doorstep
  • No change to your coverage
  • You're already approved / preapproved
  • New varieties have been released

blocks.title: You don't need to oversell it
blocks.html: Free food, already paid for, no catch. The plain truth is the strongest thing you have — which is why “how much does it cost” barely loses any calls when answered straight.

blocks.question: Which of these is approved wording?
choices: “You're already approved for up to 3 meals a day at no cost.”
“You'll get about $200 of food a month.”
blocks.explanation: Straight from the script.

blocks.html:
Never sayWhy
It costs anythingUntrue, and it loses the consumer
Their coverage changesUntrue, and it frightens people
A delivery dateYou don't know. The screener does
A dollar amountNot yours to promise
Specific meals or menusScreener's job
That you're from Medicaid or the stateYou're with America's Health
Pitch PerfectNever named on a call
And never ask for a Social Security number, a Medicaid number, or bank details. You don't need them, and asking frightens people who are right to be careful.

blocks.question: “I'm calling from Medicaid about your meal benefit.”
choices: Fine — it is a Medicaid benefit
An instant fail — you're with America's Health
blocks.explanation: The benefit is through their Medicaid; you are not Medicaid.

blocks.html: Rebutting a brush-off is the job. Pushing someone who has clearly, firmly refused is not — and on this campaign the line is drawn at a do-not-call request or a threat.

blocks.title: Swearing is not a do-not-call
blocks.html: Someone annoyed at being called is raising an objection. Stay warm, rebut, keep going. Someone telling you to stop calling is a DNC — tell them they'll be removed, end the call, and never rebuttal it.

blocks.question: “What the hell is this, why do you people keep calling?”

blocks.explanation: Annoyance is an objection. Only a stop-calling request or threat is a DNC.

modules.title: Dispositions
modules.summary: The ten codes, and the edge cases that get miscoded.

blocks.html:
CodeUse when
TransferThe screener took the call and the handoff was completed
DQNo Medicaid, copays, a non-qualifying plan, Medicare only, or outside the five boroughs
Not InterestedThey decline, or hang up after acknowledging who they are
Call BackThey ask to be called back
DNCStop calling, remove me, or a threat
Hung-Up TransferThey hang up after the transfer starts
Dead AirNo response at all
Answering MachineVoicemail — leave no message
Wrong NumberThe person asked for isn't there
No EnglishCan't continue in English

blocks.question: A consumer says “yes, that's me” then hangs up. Code?
blocks.explanation: They acknowledged, so it's Not Interested.

lessons.title: DQ is the one that matters

blocks.html: DQ is the code that protects the campaign. Five reasons: no Medicaid, copays at the doctor, a plan that isn't on the list, Medicare only, or living outside the five boroughs.

blocks.title: 38 disqualified consumers were transferred anyway
blocks.html: Out of 169 who should have been DQ'd, 99 were caught. The rest were sent to a screener who couldn't help them — wasting the screener's time and billing a transfer that shouldn't exist.
Read the DQ line, code it DQ, move to the next call. It takes ten seconds and it's a correct outcome.

blocks.question: Someone is in Yonkers. Code?
blocks.explanation: Only the five boroughs qualify.

lessons.title: The ones that get mixed up

blocks.html: Not Interested vs Dead Air: did they acknowledge? If they said anything that showed they were there, it's Not Interested. Silence throughout is Dead Air.
Not Interested vs Hung-Up Transfer: did you start the transfer? Before — Not Interested. After — Hung-Up Transfer.
Call Back vs Not Interested: “call me back” during a brush-off that you then rebut and lose is Not Interested. An actual request to be called at a specific time is a Call Back.

blocks.title: Code what happened
blocks.html: Not what you hoped happened. Miscoding patterns get noticed, and on this campaign they've cost people their seats.

blocks.question: You hit transfer, the screener's line rings, and the consumer hangs up. Code?
blocks.explanation: After the transfer starts, it's a Hung-Up Transfer.

blocks.html:
Answering Machine: you reach voicemail. Do not leave a message.

Wrong Number: the person you asked for isn't at this number. Don't pitch whoever answered — they aren't the lead and they haven't consented to anything.

blocks.question: Someone else answers and says the person you asked for doesn't live there. What do you do?
choices: Code Wrong Number and move on
blocks.explanation: They're not your lead.

questions.question: Acknowledged then hung up?
Hangs up after the transfer begins?
Pays copays at the doctor?
Lives in Jersey City?
Voicemail?
Someone else answers and the lead doesn't live there?

“Take me off your list.”

modules.title: What Real Calls Look Like
modules.summary: Patterns from 3,263 recorded calls: where they are won, where they are lost, and the five gaps that show up most.

lessons.title: Won and lost, side by side

blocks.html: Everything in this module comes from 3,263 recorded calls — 1,196 that transferred and 2,067 that didn't. Unusually, we can show you both.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hi, am I speaking with Robert? This is Dana with America's Health on a recorded line, I'm calling about the Medicaid meal service, I just need to confirm you're still receiving Medicaid —

lines.speaker: consumer
lines.text: I'm not interested.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Okay, no problem. Have a good day.

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: (Not Interested)

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: Hi, am I speaking with Robert? This is Dana with America's Health on a recorded line, calling about the Medicaid meal service. I just need to confirm you're still receiving Medicaid, correct?

lines.speaker: consumer
lines.text: I'm not interested.

lines.speaker: agent
lines.text: I understand, but groceries are NOT getting any cheaper. You are ALREADY approved for up to three meals at NO cost and this is INCLUDED in your Medicaid. I just need to confirm — you are still receiving Medicaid, correct?

lines.speaker: consumer
lines.text: ...yeah, I am.

lines.speaker: note
lines.text: (continues to borough, ZIP, double confirm, transfer)

blocks.html: Same objection, same opening. The difference is one sentence and no pause.

blocks.question: What separates the two calls above?
choices: The opening was better in the second
The agent rebutted immediately instead of accepting the no
blocks.explanation: One rebuttal, delivered without pausing.

blocks.html:
GapShare of calls
Transferred without permission32.3%
ZIP never confirmed24.7%
Medicaid question asked but talked over26.7%
Double confirm skipped18.4%
Medicaid question never asked10.4%

blocks.title: Four of the five are the same habit
blocks.html: Asking and not waiting. The question gets said, the agent keeps talking, and nothing is actually verified. The dialer records it as asked.
The fix isn't more words. It's stopping after each question until you hear an answer.

blocks.question: An agent asks about Medicaid and immediately continues into the borough question. How does that score?
choices: Asked but not waited — nothing was verified
blocks.explanation: Saying it isn't verifying it.

blocks.html:
Of the 2,067 lost calls, the loss almost always happens in one of three places:

  1. The first five seconds — consumer disengages during the identity check, before they know what the call is
  2. The first brush-off — “not interested”, “I don't need it”, “I'm busy”, unrebutted
  3. The confusion point — stacked questions with no pauses, and the consumer never understands what is being offered

blocks.title: The third one is self-inflicted
blocks.html: One real loss was summarised as: “stacked questions with no pauses; consumer never understood the offer and declined.” Slowing down is not the opposite of speed — pausing after a question is what keeps the call alive.
Say what the call is about early. A consumer who knows free meals are on the table behaves differently from one who thinks they're being sold something.

blocks.question: Where is the single most common place a call is lost?
blocks.explanation: And more than half of those got no rebuttal at all.

blocks.html: About one call in five on this campaign comes in rather than goes out. The consumer rang you.

Everything else is identical: all nine steps, the Medicaid question, the borough, the ZIP, the double confirm, permission, handoff. What changes is only the opening — don't tell someone who just called you that you're giving them a quick call.

blocks.question: On an inbound call, which steps can you skip?
blocks.explanation: Same nine steps, different opening.

lessons.title: What the best agents do differently

blocks.html:
Across the top performers' calls, three habits stand out, and none of them are clever:

  • They say what the call is about in the first sentence
  • They never let a brush-off sit — the rebuttal lands immediately
  • They stop talking after each question

blocks.title: That's it
blocks.html: No special lines, no tricks. The approved script, delivered without pauses in the wrong places and with pauses in the right ones.

blocks.question: What do the top performers have in common?
choices: They rebut immediately and wait after each question
They skip the ZIP to save time
blocks.explanation: The script, delivered properly.

modules.title: The Convoso Dialer
modules.summary: Logging in, your status, the agent screen, the transfer flow and dispositioning for the Meals campaign.

blocks.title: Use Google Chrome
blocks.html: Other browsers cause audio problems that look like dialer faults and waste your shift.

Sign in with your email and password. In the pop-up choose the Meals campaign and set your status to Available or Break, then Login.

Check the campaign every time — the wrong one means the wrong leads and the wrong script.
You are Available or Break at all times, nothing else. Allow the browser's audio permission when it asks, or calls connect to silence.
Logging out: set status to Break first (top right), then Logout at the bottom.

blocks.question: Before logging out you should…
choices: Set status to Break, then Logout
blocks.explanation: Break first, then Logout.

blocks.html:
Top left — call status, and on a live call the consumer's name and a running timer.

Top right — the blue Transfer button brings the conference tab back; the red Wrap Up button ends a call.

Left sidebar — Availability (change it before a call lands, you can't while you're on one) and the dispositions.

Tabs — Script holds your script and the conference button; Contact holds the consumer's details including their borough and ZIP.

blocks.title: Dispositioning ends the call
blocks.html: Make sure you're finished before you click, and code what actually happened.

blocks.question: Where's the conference transfer button?
blocks.explanation: On the Script tab.

blocks.html:
Once all four verifications are done and the consumer has said okay:

  1. Click the conference transfer button on the Script tab
  2. Stay on the line while it rings
  3. When the screener answers, do the warm handoff — name, borough, ZIP
  4. Wait until they're talking to each other
  5. Leave the conference, then disposition

blocks.title: The Contact tab has the borough and ZIP
blocks.html: If they've gone out of your head mid-transfer, they're one click away. Guessing the borough in a handoff is how a Queens consumer ends up with a Bronx screener.
If the consumer hangs up during the transfer, clear the screener's line first, then code it Hung-Up Transfer.

blocks.question: The consumer hangs up while the screener's line is ringing.
choices: Clear the screener's line, then code Hung-Up Transfer
blocks.explanation: Clear the line, then code it correctly.

blocks.html: Disposition every call, and code what happened. On this campaign the codes feed both pay and QA, so a miscode isn't an admin slip — it changes the numbers.

blocks.title: DQ is not a failure
blocks.html: There's a temptation to code a DQ as something softer, or to transfer it and let the screener deal with it. Both are worse than the DQ. Catching a disqualified consumer is a correct outcome and it's counted as one.
If you miscode by accident, report it simply: the number, then the correction. Keep it short and clear for QA.

blocks.question: You realise you coded a DQ as Not Interested. What do you do?
choices: Report the number and the correction to QA
blocks.explanation: Report it — short and clear.
